Complex quadratic powers and the Cauchy kernel

Reconstructed and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Earlier edition: GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Original exposition: CC0. Supplied foundations retain their stated licences.

A complex quadratic form with positive real part has a singular power that can be integrated against Schwartz tests. Its Fourier transform depends on a square root chosen continuously from the matrix, not merely from the final value of its determinant. We establish that choice, both absolute Gaussian interchanges and the full parameter domain. The planar Cauchy kernel then follows from a whole logarithmic transform, including frequency zero.

Our convention is , extended by the complex bilinear transpose. The supplied Fourier foundation, F1–F5, proves the Schwartz map, inversion, Gaussian constant and coordinate rules. Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Section 2, Lemma 2.1 and the transform proof of Theorem 3.1, supplies the full matrix branch and complex Gaussian theorem. Radial powers and the logarithmic endpoint, Theorems 1.1 and 3.1 and Lemma 3.3, supplies the radial coefficient and entire weak logarithmic gradient. The distributional linear substitution in Planar rotations and angular spectra, Theorem 1.1's proof, will be used for reflection.

For holomorphic parameters we use Complex powers at a boundary, Lemmas H0–H1, and the complete polydisk proof (C1)–(C2) in Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, Section 3. The Gamma foundation, G0–G2 and W4a–W4e, proves all scalar integral, logarithmic-moment and nonvanishing facts. The supplied finite algebra, Sections 10.1–10.6, scalar calculus, Sections 12.4–12.9, 13.1–13.5 and 13.7–13.10, integration, Sections 15.0–15.1 and 16.1–16.2, and angular foundation, A4–A5, supply the remaining matrix, convergence, substitution and polar arguments.
